newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRANCE'S TAPIE SAID CHECKING PRISON CONDITIONS.
newsitem.headline: FRANCE'S TAPIE SAID CHECKING PRISON CONDITIONS.

text.p: Bankrupt former French tycoon, politician and soccer boss Bernard Tapie was set to spend his first night in jail on Monday -- the first of many behind bars if the Supreme Court rejects his appeal on Tuesday.

By law, the fallen ex-cabinet minister, who has expressed terror at the prospect of going to jail, must report to prison on the eve of the hearing on his appeal against an eight-month sentence for rigging a soccer match.
But he still had a few possible legal emergency exits and television crews mounting guard outside Paris's La Sante prison were kept guessing whether he would actually come.
Sources close to the ex-tycoon said he would go to prison. His lawyer Jean-Yves Lienard visited the prison but declined to say what Tapie had decided.

"I wanted to discuss with the prison administration the manner in which he would be admitted to La Sante if he decided to come," Lienard told reporters. "If Mr Tapie has to go to prison, he will enter La Sante late tonight."
The lawyer added with a grin: "He won't come unless they give it a fresh coat of paint."
French media said Tapie, 54, had inquired whether he would be allowed to use his portable telephone in prison -- the answer was 'no' -- and how many showers a day he would be allowed.

He was also reported to have called Loik Le Floch Prigent, the former chairman of state railways and of oil giant Elf Aquitaine, recently released from six months in pre-trial detention, to inquire about conditions at La Sante.
VIPs in La Sante include guerrilla mastermind "Carlos".
The Supreme Court will rule on Tuesday on Tapie's final appeal against an eight-month sentence for bribing players to fix a soccer match between Marseille and Valenciennes in 1993.

If the court upholds the sentence, Tapie will stay in jail and serve the rest of his term. If it quashes his conviction, then Tapie, whose business empire once included sports equipment giant Adidas, will walk free until a re-trial.
He faces a blizzard of other legal actions over his failed holding company, tax affairs and stewardship of Marseille.
He could avoid imprisonment for several more weeks if he abandoned the appeal to the Supreme Court. Simply not turning up at the jail would annul the court hearing.
Prosecutors in Paris, where Tapie lives, would then have to determine how and when he served the sentence.
Tapie, who has begun a career as a film actor, is hoping for an open prison regime under which he could spend only nights in jail while working as an actor during the day.

Justice sources doubted that the Supreme Court would put off Tuesday's ruling because of lingering doubts about whether he is still shielded from imprisonment by his membership of the European Parliament, his last political mandate.

A French court last year ruled that he was ineligible for public office because he was personally bankrupt. But the Strasbourg-based parliament is not due to eject him formally until the start of its next plenary session on February 17.
Tapie was convicted of bribing Valenciennes players to lose to Marseille just days before his team played the 1993 European Cup Final. Marseille won the final against AC Milan by 1-0.
He is also appealing against a six-month conviction for tax fraud over his luxury yacht and will go on trial in May on charges of falsifying the accounts at Marseille.
